rows.title: The backend platform — Rules
rows.summary: 1. The platform names no dialect.
body: 1. **The platform names no dialect.** `docs/07-reference/backend.md`, the brief, `platform.toml` and the `.nuc` of
the examples hold only Nuclear and Nuclear's own library; a name of a target's library there is a bug. How a
dialect writes a kind is in that dialect's reference, never here.
2. **Kinds and features never differ between the dialects.** A feature is written once in Nuclear and every dialect
implements it: the platform's reference gets the Nuclear, each dialect's reference its output, both checks run
it. `tasks_api` must keep building with every dialect.
3. **`platform.toml` is the contract.** A kind, a decorator or a plugin a dialect uses is listed there, or the
loader refuses the dialect (N0305). The rules of a decorator are data there (`[decorators.args]`,
`[decorators.fields]`): no decorator name is written in Rust.
4. **The runtimes behave the same.** A behaviour added to one is added to the other, with the same test in both
(`packages/dragonfly-py/tests/test_data.py`, `packages/dragonfly-nest/test/data.test.ts`).
5. **A changed public API of a runtime** means its type definitions are regenerated
([runbook](docs/06-runbooks/change-a-runtime.md)).
6. **The examples are goldens.** Output that changed on purpose: `UPDATE_GOLDEN=1 cargo test`, then review the diff.

rows.title: The backend platform
rows.summary: The backend platform of Dragonfly: HTTP APIs, databases with relations, migrations and transactions, events, AI agents and graphs, written once in Nuclear and built with any of its dialects.
body: The backend platform of Dragonfly: HTTP APIs, databases with relations, migrations and transactions, events, AI
agents and graphs, written once in Nuclear and built with any of its dialects. This folder holds what is the same
for every dialect: the contract (`platform.toml`), the runtime packages the generated code runs on, the examples
and the checks. The Nuclear of a backend project never changes when its dialect changes.
Paths in these documents are relative to this folder (`nuclear-synapsis-framework/platforms/backend/`); a path that
starts with `nuclearlang/`, `nuclear-synapsis-framework/`, `tools/`, `installer/` or `.github/` starts at the root
of the tree. The rules of the whole platform are in [the root `AGENTS.md`](../../../AGENTS.md).

rows.title: Changelog — Unreleased
rows.summary: `dragonfly add|remove <package>` (ADR-lang-0008).
body: - `[toolchain] package_*` in fastapi (pip) and nestjs (npm, with the `@types` package of one that ships no types):
`dragonfly add|remove <package>` (ADR-lang-0008). `[project.manifest.advice]`: `flask`, `django`, `express`, `fastify`,
`koa` are added with a word on what the platform already gives.
- First public version.
- HTTP repositories (`Http` connection, bodiless `@get`/`@post`...) in fastapi and nestjs; `@key` for a JSON key that differs from the field; `[[generators]]` for `dragonfly gen` (ADR-codegen-0001).
- `[[generators.usecase]]`: `dragonfly gen usecase` writes a use case over a repository method, its alias in the facade and its route (ADR-codegen-0001).

- The order of a controller's routes no longer matters, in both dialects: a fixed segment wins over a parameter. Before, fastapi added the routes by method name (`GET <prefix>/search` of a generated resource answered 400, taken by `{id}`) and nestjs in the order written (`dragonfly-py` `router_of`, `dragonfly-nest` `configureApp`; `spec/backend.md` §2.7).
- `[[generators.resource]]`: the repository and the controller are merged (`merge = true`), so an action added to a resource that exists gets the members it lacks (ADR-developer-0001).

rows.title: Changelog — Unreleased
rows.summary: Unreleased
rows.body: - nestjs: `npm test` (what `dragonfly test` runs) removes `dist/test` before compiling: `tsc` never deletes the output of a source that is gone, so a test that was deleted or renamed kept running from its old `.js` and failed the project.

rows.summary: The words of this project, where one of them can be read two ways.

rows.title: Glossary
rows.summary: Glossary
body: | Term | Meaning | Not to be confused with | Where it is |
| platform | What a project writes: kinds, decorators, folders, `config.nuc`, plugins, tests. Identical for every dialect | a dialect | `platform.toml` |

| dialect | The language and framework the code comes out in: `fastapi`, `nestjs`. Chosen in `config.nuc`: `dragonfly(platform = "backend", dialect = ...)` | the platform | `nuclearlang/dialects/<language>/frameworks/<dialect>/` |
| contract of the platform | `platform.toml`: what every backend dialect must implement | the contract of an API | `platform.toml` |

| contract of an API | `.nuclear/contract.json`: the controllers, routes and models of one backend, written by its build and served by the running app; an app generates its models and repositories from it | the OpenAPI document (`.nuclear/openapi.json`, written and served beside it) | [the guide](../08-guides/contracts.md) |

| kind | The word of a declaration: `entity`, `repository`, `model`, `usecase`, `appcomponent`, `service`, `aggregate`, `controller`, `listener`, `tools`, `agent`, `state`, `graph`, `tests`, `appConfig`, `config` | a type | `[platform] kinds` |
| component | A folder `components/<name>/` of a project (`data/`, `domain/`, `api/`, `ai/`, `events/`), closed behind its facade | a UI component | `[layout]` |

rows.title: Vision — Constraints
rows.summary: readable Nuclear.
body: - The golden rule of the whole platform: generated code as fast as an expert's, instant transpilation, minimal
readable Nuclear.
- The user's rule for the data words: the code looks as much alike as possible across the platforms, at the middle
point of cost and benefit (the key decorator and `paginate` are the same word on backend and mobile).
- A feature is delivered in every dialect at once: the reference gets the Nuclear, each dialect's reference its
output, and both checks run it.

rows.title: Vision — The problem
rows.summary: A backend written in Nuclear holds only its business logic: the kinds write the framework code, the dependencies, the JSON, the validation and the routes.
body: A backend written in Nuclear holds only its business logic: the kinds write the framework code, the dependencies,
the JSON, the validation and the routes. The backend platform is the list of what such a project may write (its
kinds, decorators, folders, `config.nuc`, plugins and tests) and it is the same for every dialect, so one project
builds as the project of more than one technology and its Nuclear never changes when its dialect changes.
It covers HTTP APIs, data (entities with relations, repositories, pagination, transactions, migrations), events
and a cache, and AI (tools, agents, states, graphs).

rows.title: Vision — What it does not do
rows.summary: project.
body: - It does not say how a dialect writes its target. That is each dialect's reference, in its language's dialect
project.
- It has no kind, decorator or feature that exists in one dialect only. The one thing that ties code to a dialect is
using that dialect's type definitions (a library that exists only in its language).
- It never loads a relation by itself: no lazy query, no eager loading by default
([ADR-backend-0001](../03-adr/0001-backend-data.md)).
- It is not the `dragonfly` command: what `new`, `build`, `run`, `test` and `migrate` do is the dialect's
`[toolchain]`, run by [the command line tools](../../../../../tools/cli/AGENTS.md).
- Not there yet ([roadmap](../01-product/roadmap.md)): authentication, guards and sessions; background jobs; file
uploads; a Dockerfile; observability.

rows.title: Vision — Who uses it
rows.summary: (`nuclear help backend`) and the brief, and never a dialect's documents to know what to write.
body: - **A person or an AI agent writing a backend**: they read [the reference](../07-reference/backend.md)
(`nuclear help backend`) and [the brief](../07-reference/brief/backend.md), and never a dialect's documents to
know what to write.
- **An app of the mobile or web platform**: it gets its models and repositories generated from a backend's contract
([the guide](../08-guides/contracts.md)).
- **The author of a dialect**: `platform.toml` says what the dialect must implement; the rules of the data
decorators come with it, so a new backend dialect gets them by writing templates.
- **Whoever changes a runtime** (`packages/`): the code every generated backend runs on.

rows.title: Architecture — From a project to a running app
rows.summary: a backend project (.nuc, config.nuc) │ nuclear build . / dragonfly build ▼ the compiler ── loads ──► the dialect nuclearlang/dialects/<language>/frameworks/<dialect>/ │ └─ platform = "backend" ──► platform.toml (this folder: the contract) ▼ build/ the dialect's project, never edited ── imports ──►…
body: a backend project (.nuc, config.nuc)
│  nuclear build .  /  dragonfly build
the compiler ── loads ──► the dialect   nuclearlang/dialects/<language>/frameworks/<dialect>/
│                        └─ platform = "backend" ──► platform.toml   (this folder: the contract)
build/   the dialect's project, never edited ── imports ──► the runtime   (packages/)
│     .nuclear/contract.json, .nuclear/openapi.json
the running app: its routes, GET /.nuclear/contract.json, GET /.nuclear/openapi.json
A project has only `.nuc` files: components with `data/` (entities, repositories), `domain/` (models, use cases),
`api/` (controllers), `ai/` (tools, agents, states, graphs), `events/` (listeners) and the `appcomponent` facade;
`config/project_config.nuc` with the connections; `config.nuc` with `dragonfly(platform = "backend", dialect =
...)`, `app(...)` and `plugins(...)`; tests in `test/*_test.nuc`; errors as `Result`; Nuclear's standard library.
The rules are [the reference](../07-reference/backend.md).

rows.title: Architecture — How the data words are built

rows.title: The Python runtime: `dragonfly-py` — Data
rows.summary: How the data words of ADR-backend-0001 are built: relation that was not asked for is never queried.
body: How the data words of [ADR-backend-0001](../03-adr/0001-backend-data.md) are built:
- **Relations**: `many_to_one`, `one_to_many`, `many_to_many`, `one_to_one` in `orm.py`, all `lazy="raise"`: a
relation that was not asked for is never queried. The foreign key is appended to the table in
`Entity.__init_subclass__`. Join tables are made when the mappers are configured, so `Database.open` calls
`configure_mappers()`; SQLite runs `PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON`.
- **Answers**: `to_dict` and `EntitySchema` leave an unloaded relation out.
- **What the generated project gives the runtime**: `main.py` and `conftest.py` list every entity
(`entities=[...]`), so SQLAlchemy knows all the tables; two entities that name each other are imported only for
the type checker (`if TYPE_CHECKING:`).
- **Transactions**: a session kept in a `ContextVar`, which `Repository.use()` joins.
- **Defaults**: a field's default is also the column's SQL default (`column(default=...)` sets `server_default`),
so a non-null column can be added to a table that has rows.

rows.title: The Python runtime: `dragonfly-py` — Migrations
rows.summary: `dragonfly.migrate` runs Alembic for `dragonfly migrate` (the dialect's `[toolchain]` keys `migrate_make`, `migrate`, `migrate_down`): python -m dragonfly.migrate make "add done to tasks" --dir <migrations> # one migration: the entities minus the last one python -m dragonfly.migrate up --dir…
body: `dragonfly.migrate` runs Alembic for `dragonfly migrate` (the dialect's `[toolchain]` keys `migrate_make`,
`migrate`, `migrate_down`):
```sh
python -m dragonfly.migrate make "add done to tasks" --dir <migrations>   # one migration: the entities minus the last one
python -m dragonfly.migrate up --dir <migrations>                         # applies the pending ones
python -m dragonfly.migrate down --dir <migrations>                       # reverts the last one
- `make` never reads the database: it brings an empty SQLite in memory to the last migration and lets Alembic's
autogenerate write the difference.
- The folder is an Alembic script folder (`env.py`, `script.py.mako`, `versions/`), written the first time.
- `up` and `down` use the default database of the app's configuration, which `create_app` keeps in `app.state`;
`alembic_version` lists what is applied.
- Migrations are written in batch mode, so SQLite (which cannot alter a column) and the other databases run the
same file.

rows.title: The TypeScript runtime: `dragonfly-nest` — Data
rows.summary: How the data words of ADR-backend-0001 are built: `save` writes a `@manyToOne` that is set to a row and `$set`s a `@manyToMany` list.
body: How the data words of [ADR-backend-0001](../03-adr/0001-backend-data.md) are built:
- **Relations**: the runtime's `Entity` base keeps the relations given to the constructor (sequelize drops them).
`save` writes a `@manyToOne` that is set to a row and `$set`s a `@manyToMany` list. Only the side with the column
declares the foreign key (`constraints: false` on `@HasMany` / `@HasOne`). `joinTable(name, fk, other)` makes the
join table (no timestamps).
- **Types**: `Related<T>` types a single relation, so the decorator metadata never reads the other class (two ES
modules that import each other).
- **Transactions**: an `AsyncLocalStorage` whose transaction every repository call passes as `{ transaction }`. It
opens on the database of the last repository made ([roadmap](../01-product/roadmap.md)).

rows.title: The TypeScript runtime: `dragonfly-nest` — Entry points and modules
rows.summary: Behaviour worth knowing: client still loads the base (they are optional peers: dependencies).
body: Behaviour worth knowing:
- The entry points are apart so a production install without `@nestjs/testing`, the AI libraries or a broker's
client still loads the base (they are optional peers: [dependencies](dependencies.md)).
- `ChromaStore` is chromadb's client behind a LangChain `VectorStore`. `@langchain/community` was rejected: its
peers conflict with zod 4 and ioredis 6.
- The order of a controller's routes does not matter: a fixed segment wins over a parameter (`configureApp`;
reference §2.7).
- In the tests the databases are SQLite in memory (`DRAGONFLY_DATABASE=memory`, set by `startTestApp`).

as a copy, never as a link:
```sh
npm install --no-save --install-links <path to>/packages/dragonfly-nest
A symlink resolves the runtime's peers in its own `node_modules`, and two copies of `@nestjs/common` break `tsc`.

rows.title: The TypeScript runtime: `dragonfly-nest` — Migrations
rows.summary: Sequelize has no autogenerate, so the runtime brings its own (`src/migrate.ts`, bin `dragonfly-nest-migrate`), run by `dragonfly migrate` after `tsc` (the dialect's `[toolchain]` keys `migrate_make`, `migrate`, `migrate_down`): npx dragonfly-nest-migrate make "add done to tasks" --dir <migrations>…
body: Sequelize has no autogenerate, so the runtime brings its own (`src/migrate.ts`, bin `dragonfly-nest-migrate`), run
by `dragonfly migrate` after `tsc` (the dialect's `[toolchain]` keys `migrate_make`, `migrate`, `migrate_down`):
```sh
npx dragonfly-nest-migrate make "add done to tasks" --dir <migrations>   # one migration: the entities minus the last one
npx dragonfly-nest-migrate up --dir <migrations>                         # applies the pending ones
npx dragonfly-nest-migrate down --dir <migrations>                       # reverts the last one
- It reads the `entities` and the `config` the app module exports.
- `schemaOf` reads the entities' attributes, `diff` compares them with the `schema` the last migration exports (so
`make` never reads the database), `render` writes `up` / `down` over `queryInterface`.
- Applied migrations are listed in `SequelizeMeta` (sequelize-cli's table). umzug was not needed.

rows.title: Testing — Conventions
rows.summary: dialect runs with its own runner; a behaviour of the runtimes has the same test in both (`packages/dragonfly-py/tests/test_data.py`, `packages/dragonfly-nest/test/data.test.ts`).
body: - **One feature, both dialects.** A feature has a test in Nuclear in the example (`test/*_test.nuc`), which each
dialect runs with its own runner; a behaviour of the runtimes has the same test in both
(`packages/dragonfly-py/tests/test_data.py`, `packages/dragonfly-nest/test/data.test.ts`).
- **Goldens.** When the generated output changes on purpose: `UPDATE_GOLDEN=1 cargo test`, then review the diff. An
expected file the build no longer produces is a failure too.
- **No network, no real service.** The checks use SQLite (in memory or a temporary file) and fake chat models
(`FakeModel`). What was never run against a real service is listed in the roadmaps (this one and each
dialect's).
- **The tests of a project start from an empty database**: in memory, empty in each test.

rows.title: Testing — Running the checks
rows.summary: cargo test sh nuclear-synapsis-framework/platforms/backend/checks/fastapi-check/check.sh sh nuclear-synapsis-framework/platforms/backend/checks/nestjs-check/check.sh Both scripts find the tree from their own place (`NUCLEAR_ROOT` overrides it), build with `cargo run -p nuclear-cli -- build` and…
body: ```sh
cargo test
sh nuclear-synapsis-framework/platforms/backend/checks/fastapi-check/check.sh
sh nuclear-synapsis-framework/platforms/backend/checks/nestjs-check/check.sh
Both scripts find the tree from their own place (`NUCLEAR_ROOT` overrides it), build with
`cargo run -p nuclear-cli -- build` and stop at the first failure, printing the failed command's whole output.
**`fastapi-check/check.sh`**, in order:
1. Builds `examples/examples-fastapi/rick_api` into its `build/`.
2. pyright over the generated project, then its tests (pytest: the project's `test/*_test.nuc`).
3. `smoke.py`: the REST API over an in-memory database (201, 409, 400, 404, the list), the agent with its tools and
the graph with a fake chat model (no network), and `/openapi.json`.
4. The runtime's tests: `packages/dragonfly-py/tests`.
5. **Conformance**: copies `examples/examples-backend/tasks_api` (written for `nestjs`), switches its `config.nuc`
to `dialect = "fastapi"`, builds it, runs pyright and its tests.
6. **Migrations**: on that copy, with `DATABASE` set to a fresh SQLite file, `dragonfly.migrate make "first"`,
`up`, then `make "again"` must answer "no changes".
**`nestjs-check/check.sh`**, in order:

rows.title: Testing — Running the checks
rows.summary: 1. Builds the runtime with `tsc` and copies it fresh into `nuclearlang/tools/node/node_modules` (`npm install --no-save --install-links`).
body: 1. Builds the runtime with `tsc` and copies it fresh into `nuclearlang/tools/node/node_modules`
(`npm install --no-save --install-links`). npm keeps an old copy of the same version, so the script removes it
first; a `--no-save` install also prunes the other runtime installed the same way, so the web platform's check
installs its own again.
2. Builds `examples/examples-backend/tasks_api` and links `node_modules` into its `build/`.
3. `tsc --strict`, then the project's tests (`node --test "dist/test/**/*.js"`).
4. `smoke.mjs`: the REST CRUD over SQLite in memory (`DRAGONFLY_DATABASE=memory`), validation (400 with two
messages), the errors of a `Result` (409, 404).
5. **Migrations**: with `DATABASE` set to a fresh SQLite file, `migrate make "first"`, `up`, then `make "again"`
must answer "no changes".
6. The runtime's tests (`tsconfig.test.json`, `dist-test/test/**/*.js`).

| The nestjs check | the runtime built; `tasks_api` built; `tsc --strict` and the project's own tests; a live run; the migrations | `checks/nestjs-check/check.sh` |
| The references' equivalences | each dialect's reference against the real output (the dialects' projects own them) | `nuclearlang/tools/spec-check/check.py` |

rows.summary: A behaviour of the platform exists in both packages, with the same test in both (`packages/dragonfly-py/tests/test_data.py`, `packages/dragonfly-nest/test/data.test.ts`).

(`packages/dragonfly-py/tests/test_data.py`, `packages/dragonfly-nest/test/data.test.ts`).

rows.title: After changing a runtime — 2. Build and install the changed runtime
rows.summary: sources, nothing to repeat.
body: - **`dragonfly-py`** is installed in `nuclearlang/tools/python/.venv` with `pip install -e`: the venv reads the
sources, nothing to repeat.
- **`dragonfly-nest`** is compiled and copied, never linked. The nestjs check does both; by hand:
```sh
(cd nuclear-synapsis-framework/platforms/backend/packages/dragonfly-nest && npm install && npx tsc -p tsconfig.json)
(cd nuclearlang/tools/node && npm install --no-save --install-links ../../../nuclear-synapsis-framework/platforms/backend/packages/dragonfly-nest)
The install is repeated after every rebuild: a symlink would resolve the runtime's peers in its own
`node_modules`, and two copies of `@nestjs/common` break `tsc`.

rows.title: After changing a runtime — 4. A changed public API: regenerate the type definitions
rows.summary: The compiler and the editors know the runtimes' names from their type definitions.
body: The compiler and the editors know the runtimes' names from their type definitions.
```sh
nuclearlang/tools/defs/python/generate.sh        # nuclearlang/dialects/python/defs/, from nuclearlang/tools/python/.venv
nuclearlang/tools/defs/typescript/generate.sh    # nuclearlang/dialects/typescript/defs/, from nuclearlang/tools/node/node_modules
Each script regenerates every package of its language with the versions installed there, the runtime among them
(`dragonfly`, `dragonfly-nest`). If a version changed, update the `defs` lists of the dialects
(`nuclearlang/dialects/python/dialect.toml` and `frameworks/fastapi/dialect.toml`;
`nuclearlang/dialects/typescript/frameworks/nestjs/dialect.toml`). Then `cargo test`.

rows.title: After changing a runtime — 5. Goldens, documents, the installed copy
rows.summary: `CHANGELOG.md` a line.
body: - The generated output changed: `UPDATE_GOLDEN=1 cargo test`, and review the diff.
- A change a user can see: `docs/07-reference/backend.md` gets the Nuclear, each dialect's reference its output,
`CHANGELOG.md` a line.
- `installer/install.sh`: the installed `dragonfly` installs the runtimes into a project from the installation's
`packages/`, so a project of the user sees the change only after it.
Publishing the packages (PyPI, npm) is not set up yet: [roadmap](../01-product/roadmap.md).

rows.title: Contracts: one backend, its apps generated — 1. The backend publishes its contract
rows.summary: Nothing to write.
body: Nothing to write. Building the backend (`nuclear build .`, `dragonfly build`, or the editor when it checks the
project) writes two files next to the project card:
| File | Holds |

| `.nuclear/contract.json` | the controllers and their routes (verb, path, parameters and where each goes, body, answer, error, status), the models those carry (fields, Nuclear types, defaults, JSON names, validation rules, the key field, doc comments) |
| `.nuclear/openapi.json` | the same as OpenAPI 3.1, for Swagger UI, generators or an HTTP tool |
Both are copied into `build/` and the running API serves them at `GET /.nuclear/contract.json` and
`GET /.nuclear/openapi.json`. The contract is the same whether the backend is built with `fastapi` or `nestjs`.
```nuclear
// tasks_api/components/tasks/api/tasks_controller.nuc
// The CRUD of tasks.
@controller("tasks")
controller TasksController(tasks: TasksAppComponent)
@get("{id}")
one(id: int) Result<Error, Task>
~tasks.task(id)
@post()
create(input: NewTask) Result<Error, Task>
~tasks.create(input)

rows.title: Contracts: one backend, its apps generated — 2. The app declares the backend
rows.summary: One line in the app's `config.nuc`, and a connection with the same name: // tasks_app/config.nuc dragonfly(platform = "mobile", dialect = "flutter") app(name = "tasks_app", version = "1.0.0+1") contracts(tasks_api = "../tasks_api") // the backend checked out next to the app //…
body: One line in the app's `config.nuc`, and a connection with the same name:
```nuclear
// tasks_app/config.nuc
dragonfly(platform = "mobile", dialect = "flutter")
app(name = "tasks_app", version = "1.0.0+1")
contracts(tasks_api = "../tasks_api")              // the backend checked out next to the app
// tasks_app/config/project_config.nuc
appConfig ProjectConfig
connections: Connection[] = [
Http(connectionName = "tasks_api", baseUrl = "http://localhost:3000/"),
**Not a monorepo?** Point at the running API instead and fetch the contract when you want to follow a change:
```nuclear
contracts(tasks_api = "https://api.example.com")
```sh
nuclear contracts update          # GET https://api.example.com/.nuclear/contract.json → contracts/tasks_api/
nuclear contracts list            # each contract, its source, the version of the copy
The copy (`contracts/tasks_api/contract.json`) is committed with the app: a build never needs the network, and the
diff of a commit shows exactly what changed in the API.

rows.title: Contracts: one backend, its apps generated — 3. What the build generates
rows.summary: `contracts/tasks_api/` is written at every build (a path) or by `contracts update` (a url); the files say they are generated.
body: `contracts/tasks_api/` is written at every build (a path) or by `contracts update` (a url); the files say they
are generated. The mobile example `examples/examples-flutter-dialect/tasks_app` gets:
```nuclear
// contracts/tasks_api/models/task.nuc
Task
@primary
id: int
title: string
done: boolean = false
// 1 high, 2 normal, 3 low
priority: int = 2
createdAt?: DateTime
// contracts/tasks_api/models/new_task.nuc
NewTask
@maxLength(200)
@minLength(1)
title: string
@max(3)
@min(1)
priority: int = 2
// contracts/tasks_api/tasks_repository.nuc
@repository(path = "tasks", connection = "tasks_api")
repository TasksRepository
@get(local = true)
all(done?: boolean) Result<TasksApiError, Task[]>
@get(path = ":id", local = true)
one(id: int) Result<TasksApiError, Task>
@post
create(input: NewTask) Result<TasksApiError, Task>
The rules of `NewTask` came from the backend: a form on it refuses what the API refuses. `Task` has its key, so
the GETs get `local = true` and `allAsLocal()` / `oneAsLocal()` answer offline. Only what the app's platform
understands is written (a web app gets no `@primary` and no rules until it has forms and a local database).

(tasks: TasksRepository)

rows.summary: The Nuclear HTTP view of the VS Code extension lists every project of the workspace by platform, its components and endpoints (from the contracts), the contracts an app declares with an *Update* action, and OpenAPI documents of APIs that are not Nuclear.
body: The **Nuclear HTTP** view of the VS Code extension lists every project of the workspace by platform, its
components and endpoints (from the contracts), the contracts an app declares with an *Update* action, and OpenAPI
documents of APIs that are not Nuclear. Clicking an endpoint opens a request panel with the active environment's
variables and headers (`.nuclear/http.json`), a sample body built from the model, and the pretty-printed response.
Rules: [projects.md §1.2](../../../../../nuclearlang/docs/07-reference/projects.md); plan and decisions: `specs/003-shared-contracts/plan.md`,
ADR-synapsis-0006.

rows.title: Contracts: one backend, its apps generated
rows.summary: A backend written in Nuclear describes its API once.
body: A backend written in Nuclear describes its API once. Every app that calls it (mobile, web) gets the models and
the repositories **generated from that description** instead of writing them by hand, and a change in the API is
caught when the app builds, not on the phone (ADR-synapsis-0006). Backend and app stay two projects, deployed apart, talking
over HTTP: what travels is a JSON description, as OpenAPI or a `.proto` file would.
